segments.original: Flashback to 1956. A series of short, low-budget British documentaries reaches London screens. As one London newspaper put it, "all the bearded boys in duffel coats and the girls in jeans with cropped hair in the city seem to converge" on the South Bank to watch "Free Cinema" films.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The documentaries frankly tackled subjects such as amusement parks, dance halls, and youth clubs. In the context of British cinema at the time, they were pioneering works. For director and critic Lindsay Anderson (1923-1994), the 1950s were, for British cinema, a period of complacency and "lukewarm humanism". It was the era of John Mills war films and stoic dramas in which "chaps" like Jack Hawkins appeared smoking pipes.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The British New Wave was driven by a group of critics turned filmmakers who, in the late 1940s, were closely linked to the film magazine Sequence, at the University of Oxford, and later went on to write for Sight and Sound. Its leading figures were Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz (1926-2002), Tony Richardson (1928-1991), and Gavin Lambert (1924-2005). In their first feature films, the group resolutely turned its focus to the industrial north of Britain.
segments.text: The British New Wave was driven by a group of critics turned filmmakers who, in the late nineteen forties, were closely linked to the film magazine Sequence, at the University of Oxford, and later went on to write for Sight and Sound. Its leading figures were Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz (nineteen twenty-six to two thousand two), Tony Richardson (nineteen twenty-eight to nineteen ninety-one), and Gavin Lambert (nineteen twenty-four to two thousand five). In their first feature films, the group resolutely turned its focus to the industrial north of Britain.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: But the film most widely accepted as the starting point of the British New Wave was made by Jack Clayton (1921-1995), a director not linked to the Sequence group. The subversive northern working-class hero and the unprecedentedly direct treatment of sex and social class in Room at the Top (1958) set the template followed by Reisz in Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1960), Richardson in The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner (1962), and Anderson in This Sporting Life (1963).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Like Clayton, John Schlesinger (1926-2003) also kept his distance from the core group, but his A Kind of Loving (1962), starring Alan Bates (1934-2003), follows the same pattern. All these films were made, as Richardson later wrote, with "a minimum of equipment, real locations, and a naturally unkempt look".

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Most British New Wave films are adaptations of novels and plays, as is the case with Look Back in Anger (1959) and A Taste of Honey (1961) - both by Tony Richardson (1928-1991) - based respectively on Look Back in Anger, by John Osborne, and A Taste of Honey, by Shelagh Delaney.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: As expected, the energy of the British New Wave soon dissipated. Before leaving for Hollywood, Tony Richardson made the period extravaganza Tom Jones (1963). After Billy Liar (1963), Schlesinger turned his attention south with Darling (1965). The far-from-prolific Anderson made no other film until if.... (1968). But the spirit of the New Wave transformed British cinema forever. Its influence can be seen in the films of Ken Loach (b. 1936), Mike Leigh (b. 1943), and Terence Davies (b. 1945) and, more recently, in the work of Andrea Arnold (b. 1961), Lynne Ramsay (b. 1969), and Pawel Pawlikowski (b. 1957).
